questions.question: A map contains 80 GiB of primary data and has two backups. How much raw map data is stored before overhead and recovery reserve?
options: 80 GiB
160 GiB
240 GiB
320 GiB
questions.explanation: The primary plus two backups are three complete copies: 80 x 3 = 240 GiB before object overhead, indexes, and recovery headroom.

questions.question: What changes when a map backup is asynchronous instead of synchronous?
options: The backup no longer consumes memory
The mutation can return before the backup copy catches up
The map becomes a CP data structure
The key is assigned to a different partition
questions.explanation: An asynchronous backup is not on the blocking acknowledgement path. That can reduce write latency but leaves a window in which the primary is newer than its backup.

questions.question: Which workload most clearly calls for a CP Subsystem primitive?
options: A rebuildable product-card cache
A best-effort analytics projection
A fencing decision that must have only one current owner
A local copy of public documentation
questions.explanation: Fencing and coordination require one authoritative order. A Raft-backed CP primitive sacrifices minority availability to preserve that property.

questions.question: What does split-brain protection do for a configured AP map?
options: It instantly repairs the failed network
It rejects protected operations when observed membership is below the configured minimum
It converts every map write into a Raft transaction
It guarantees no detection delay
questions.explanation: Minimum-size protection can reject selected operations after the cluster observes insufficient membership. It does not remove failure-detection delay or turn an AP structure into a CP one.

questions.question: Why can a Near Cache return stale data even when the cluster map is healthy?
options: Every Near Cache read bypasses its local copy
The client holds another copy whose invalidation or reconnect path can lag
Near Cache entries are always durable
Partition keys are encrypted locally
questions.explanation: A Near Cache is an additional client-side copy. Invalidation, missed messages, reconnect repair, TTL, and eviction determine its real freshness window.

questions.question: What is the safest way to handle an external side effect from an at-least-once stream?
options: Assume every record arrives exactly once
Use a stable event identity and an idempotent or deduplicating sink
Disable snapshots and retries
Increase the map backup count only
questions.explanation: At-least-once recovery may replay records. Stable identity and sink-side idempotency contain duplicate business effects across retry and restart.

questions.question: Which test best proves that a backup-count setting is operationally affordable?
options: Read the configuration file only
Remove a member under peak load and measure migration, latency, memory, and safety restoration
Check average CPU while the cluster is idle
Count the number of map names
questions.explanation: The real cost appears during failure: surviving members absorb ownership, migrate data, and rebuild backups while continuing application traffic.
